theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Moral Law and the Christian
doctrine: The Moral Law and the Christian
summary: The three uses of the law; the law as it applies to the believer under grace; the law fulfilled in love
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 20:1-17, Matthew 5:17-48, and Romans 13:8-10. The first is the Ten Commandments, the second is Jesus’ teaching about the law in the Sermon on the Mount, and the third is Paul’s summary of the law as love. Read them in order, and ask how each one relates to the others.
settingTheScene: This is the second doctrinal pause in Unit 5, and it raises one of the most important questions in the Christian life: what is the place of the law for someone who is saved by grace? Christians have debated this for two thousand years. Some say that Christ has abolished the law. Others say that it applies to us just as it did to Israel. The answer, as usual, is in between, and it takes careful reading. You are not under the law as a way of earning salvation, and yet the law still matters. This day will help you see how.
observation: The Ten Commandments begin with grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2).
Jesus says, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17).
“Until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota or a dot will pass from the Law until all is accomplished” (5:18).
Jesus teaches six times, “You have heard that it was said…But I say to you” (5:21, 27, 31, 33, 38, 43).

On murder: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (5:22). On adultery: “Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (5:28).
He ends: “You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (5:48).
Paul writes, “Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13:8).
The commandments “are summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (13:9). “Love is the fulfilling of the law” (13:10).
doctrinalFocus:
Christians have long spoken of three uses of the law, a framework that goes back to the Reformation. The first use is civil or political. The law restrains evil in society by setting boundaries and threatening punishment. Paul says that the law is “not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient” (1 Timothy 1:9). The second use is pedagogical, or evangelical. The law shows us our sin and drives us to Christ. Paul writes, “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20), and “the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24). The third use is for believers: the law shows what a life that pleases God looks like. It guides the redeemed to live as the redeemed.

You can see all three at work in Exodus 19 and 20. The commandments restrain a violent and idolatrous people. They also expose sin, as the people’s quick fall into idolatry proves. And they tell a freed people how to live as God’s people. All three uses are present.

How does this fit with the New Testament? Here the Bible’s own storyline matters. The law given at Sinai was a covenant with Israel, with its own sanctions, rituals, and civil laws. The New Testament teaches that Christians are no longer “under the law” in that sense (Romans 6:14; Galatians 3:25). The Mosaic covenant, as a covenant, has been fulfilled and replaced by the new covenant (Hebrews 8:13). This means that we do not keep the sacrificial system, the food laws, or the civil code of ancient Israel. They pointed to Christ, and he has accomplished what they signified.

But this does not mean that the moral will of God has changed. Jesus says that he came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it. He fulfilled it in several ways: by obeying it perfectly, by bearing its penalty, by fulfilling what it pointed to, and by revealing its deepest meaning. In the Sermon on the Mount, he shows that the commandments reach the heart: not just murder but anger, not just adultery but lust. The moral core of the Ten Commandments is reaffirmed in the New Testament, though now seen in the light of Christ, and nine of the ten are repeated explicitly (the fourth, about the Sabbath, is applied in a distinctive way through the rest we have in Christ, as in Hebrews 4:9-10 and Colossians 2:16-17).

The new covenant also gives something the old could not: a new heart. Jeremiah promised, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). This is the power of the Spirit. The law still shows us what God desires, but now the Spirit enables us to love it. Paul calls this “the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2), the law of love as lived and taught by Jesus.

That is why Paul can say in Romans 13 that love fulfills the law. He does not mean that love replaces the commandments. He means that love is what the commandments were pointing to all along. If you love your neighbor, you will not murder, steal, or covet. The law is not a list of rules to be checked. It is a description of what love does.
interpretation:
Pay attention to what Jesus does in Matthew 5. He does not loosen the law. He tightens it. Anger is a kind of murder. Lust is a kind of adultery. This is not meant to crush his hearers into despair, though it does that for anyone honest. It is meant to show that the standard is perfection, “as your heavenly Father is perfect.” No one can meet that standard. The law is a mirror that shows us what we are.

But this is where the good news comes in. If you cannot keep the law, you need someone who has. Jesus lived a life of perfect obedience, and he gives it to those who trust in him. In 2 Corinthians 5:21, Paul says, “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” Our standing before God is based on his obedience, not ours.

And once you are in Christ, the law takes on a new character. It is no longer a threat. It is a guide. It describes the kind of life that the Spirit is producing in you. This is why Paul can say both that we are not under the law and that we fulfill its requirement (Romans 8:4). The one who is saved by grace wants to obey.

The structure of Exodus 20 should be remembered. Grace comes first: “I brought you out.” Then law: “You shall.” This is the order of the gospel. We obey because we have been saved, not in order to be saved.
connection: Romans 8:3-4 says that “God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do…in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.” Galatians 5:14 says, “For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” James 2:8-12 calls it “the royal law” and “the law of liberty.” Hebrews 8:10 quotes Jeremiah 31 about the law written on the heart.
application:
Read the Sermon on the Mount slowly this week. Ask the Spirit to show you where your heart does not match the standard, and bring that to Christ.

Choose one commandment to meditate on, and ask how a person who loves God and neighbor would keep it in your situation this week.

Thank God for the new heart he has given you, and ask him to increase your delight in his commands.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that the law shows your need and drives you to Christ.
Ask the Spirit to write his law on your heart.
Ask for a love for God and neighbor that comes from the heart.
